answer:
Because a per-hop timeout bounds only one wait, and a chain of separate caps never adds up to the caller's budget. Individually reasonable values still overrun the end-to-end deadline through five compounding effects.

1) Composition is not a budget. Independent per-hop timeouts limit different operations; for sequential hops the worst case is their sum, plus retries. The book's hypothetical 900 ms request budget partitioned into 50 ms edge/auth, 100 ms queueing, 450 ms downstream, 100 ms durable write and 200 ms margin notes that per-hop independent 900 ms timeouts 'would allow the aggregate to vastly exceed the caller's deadline.' Each hop should use at most the remaining deadline minus its own processing and margin, then propagate the remainder.

2) Retries and backoff spend the same budget repeatedly. Each attempt consumes the remaining deadline and attempt budget, and retries at proxy, API and downstream layers compound into a 'combinatorial retry explosion'; a timeout that silently becomes a retry multiplies load, and jitter/backoff delay can spend budget after the result stopped being useful. An exponential curve without a deadline check can outlive usefulness.

3) Key segments are outside the timed region. The deadline must include admission, executor queue wait, connection acquisition, execution and response transfer, yet a socket/read timeout typically starts after queueing. A bounded pool with an unbounded queue can add latency while reporting few immediate errors, so per-hop numbers look fine while elapsed time does not.

4) Fan-out amplifies tails. When a parent waits for all of N parallel dependencies, a per-hop threshold met by each child 99% of the time gives 0.99^10 ≈ 90.4% composed success for ten calls and about 60.5% for fifty: some branch exceeds its 'reasonable' timeout far more often than the per-hop number suggests. Percentiles do not add, and a shared pool, lock or executor can re-serialize nominally parallel branches.

5) Enforcement is optional and expiry does not stop work. A propagated deadline without an enforcement point is only a hint; clock skew, a lost header or a hop that ignores expiry breaks it. Expiry does not undo a committed effect or necessarily halt downstream work, because cancellation is cooperative; the caller can abandon the request while servers keep working, and detached work must get its own durable deadline rather than inherit the request's remaining time.

Therefore the chain outlives the deadline: budget is consumed where per-hop timeouts do not measure (queueing, connection acquisition, response transfer) and in multiples they do not model (retries, fan-out tails), while enforcement and cancellation are best-effort. The remedy is one end-to-end deadline, propagated and enforced at every hop with remaining-time arithmetic, retries charged against it at a single layer, queue and pool waits counted inside it, and durable reconciliation for effects that outlive the response.
